guides.title: #01 Chart Setup
guides.line: Volume profile, VWAP and ATR on your chart.
pages: CHART SETUP Volume profile · VWAP · ATR

CHART SETUP PART 01 The Volume Profile Fixed range volume profile — the tool everything else hangs off. 1.1 Find the tool On the drawing toolbar down the left of the chart, click the icon above the paintbrush. Under VOLUME-BASED, choose Fixed range volume profile. Hit the star next to it so it sits in your favourites — you’ll be drawing this on every session. 2

CHART SETUP 1.2 Set the inputs Right-click the profile once it’s drawn and open Settings. Row Size 1000 gives you enough resolution to actually see the shelves rather than a blurry blob. Volume: Up/Down splits buying and selling. Value Area Volume 70 is the standard 70% of trade, which is what makes the VAH and VAL mean anything. Leave Extend Right unchecked so the profile stays on its own range instead of projecting across the chart. The one exception is the developing profile — on that one you tick Extend Right, so the developing levels carry across to where price is trading now. 3

CHART SETUP 1.3 Set the style Width 30 and Placement Left keeps the histogram out of the way of price. Values off — the numbers are clutter. Turn VAH and VAL on in blue and POC on in red, so the three lines you actually trade are instantly separable. Leave Developing POC and Developing VA off here; this profile is for pre-existing levels, not the developing one. 4

CHART SETUP 1.4 Colour the volume Click the Up Volume and Down Volume swatches and set both to the same green at 50% opacity. Then set Value Area Up and Value Area Down to teal at 75%. Same colour for up and down is deliberate — I’m reading where volume built, not who built it — and the darker value area makes the 70% block jump out of the rest of the profile. 1.5 What you should end up with A profile sitting on the left of its range, a red POC, two blue value area lines, and a darker block showing where the bulk of the business got done. If you can see the shelves at a glance without squinting, it’s set up right. 5

CHART SETUP PART 02 VWAP Session fair value, with three bands of stretch. 2.1 Add the indicator Open Indicators at the top of the chart and search for Volume-weighted average price. Star it while you’re there. 6

CHART SETUP 2.2 Set the inputs Anchor Period: Session so it resets every session and only ever shows you this session’s fair value. Source: (H + L + C) / 3 — the typical price, so each bar contributes the middle of its range rather than just its close. Bands Calculation Mode: Standard Deviation, with multipliers 1, 2 and 3, so band width scales with the session’s own volatility instead of a fixed distance. Wait for timeframe closes on, so nothing repaints while a bar is forming. 7

CHART SETUP 2.3 Set the style Turn on VWAP and all three Upper / Lower Band pairs, with a different colour per band so you can tell at a glance how stretched price is. Leave all three Bands Fill boxes off — the shading buries the profile underneath. 8
CHART SETUP PART 03 ATR One number, used for stop size. 3.1 Add the indicator Indicators → Average true range. 9

CHART SETUP 3.2 Set the inputs Length 60 with RMA smoothing. A 60-period average on your execution chart is slow enough that the number doesn’t jump around between trades, which matters because the stop rule depends on it. Wait for timeframe closes on, same reason as VWAP. 3.3 Set the style and use it One line, in a colour you can read off the bottom panel at a glance. The reason it’s on the chart at all: stop loss at ATR × 2, which gives the trade enough room to breathe without guessing at stop size. 10

CHART SETUP PA R T 0 4 Marking Your Levels Set up your templates once, then mark every level in a few clicks. Everything is on the 1-minute chart. All profiles and levels are drawn on the 1-minute chart, and we execute on the 1-minute chart too. Type the level's name, here NYVAH, and set the alignment to Middle and Right so the label sits at the right end of the ray, next to price. 11

CHART SETUP 4.9 What you should end up with A ray running right from the level, labelled NYVAH, so it's waiting on your chart for the next session. Repeat for the POC and VAL, then do the same for the overnight and prior week profiles. WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · THE OVERNIGHT VAH 4.10 Draw the overnight profile Same process, different window. The overnight session runs from 18:00 to 09:29 ET, so the profile goes from the 18:00 bar on Thursday evening to the 09:29 bar on Friday morning. 15

CHART SETUP 4.11 Put a ray on the VAH The overnight VAH is the blue line at the top of the profile's value area, here at 7,662.25. Click right on it to place the ray. 4.12 Apply the ONVAH template Templates on the ray's toolbar, then ONVAH. The ray turns overnight orange and picks up its label. 16

CHART SETUP 4.13 Two levels marked The orange ONVAH now sits above the NYVAH from the first example. Every level goes on the same way. Only the session window and the template change. 4.14 Your finished chart: nine lines Do this for every level and your chart should end up with nine lines: NY in red, overnight in orange and prior week in white. This is just an example from Friday 13 Nov. Your levels will be different every day, so you mark the NY and overnight levels fresh before each session. The exception is the prior week levels: you mark them once at the start of the week and they carry over from Monday to Friday. KEY TA KEAWAY Profile, ray, template. Three profiles, nine levels, marked the same way every time. 17

guides.title: #03 Volume Profile 101
guides.line: How the auction works, and why our levels matter.
pages: VOLUME PROFILE 101 How the auction works, and why our levels matter VP ACADEMY · 03

VP ACADEMY #03 S TA RTHERE One idea Everything in this system comes back to it. Price moves to find where business gets done. That's the whole idea behind volume profile. The market is always looking for the price where buyers and sellers are both happy to trade. When it finds one, volume builds there. When it doesn't, price gets pushed away. Every level we mark (NYVAH, ONPOC, PWVAL, dPOC and the rest) is just a price where the market already found that agreement. That's why price reacts when it comes back to them. W H AT ' SINSIDE PA R T The auction 01 How price finds value, and what happens inside it vs outside it PA R T 02 PA R T 03 Reading a profile POC, VAH, VAL and HVN, and why above the dVAH is expensive and below the dVAL is cheap Our levels and setups The four profiles we mark, how they stack into a grade, and the Snap, Flip and Magnet 2

VP ACADEMY #03 PA R T 0 1 The Auction Price is always testing for a fair deal. Think of a durian stall. Price them too high and nobody buys, so the price comes down. Price them too low and they sell out, so the price goes up. Most durians get sold at the price in between, where both sides are happy. TOO EXPENSIVE PRICE Buyers walk away. Nobody trades, so price has to come down. FAIR VALUE Buyers and sellers both happy. This is where most trade happens. TOO CHEAP Buyers rush in. Stock runs out, so price has to go up. NQ works the same way, just much faster. Price moves up looking for sellers and down looking for buyers. Where both sides agree, trading slows and volume builds. Where nobody wants to trade, price gets pushed away fast. KEY TA KEAWAY Lots of volume at a price means the market accepted it. Very little volume means it rejected it. 3

VP ACADEMY #03 PA R T 0 1 Inside Value or Leaving It The market only ever does one of two things. Most of the time price is in balance: rotating inside a range because both sides agree on value. Then one side takes over, price breaks out (imbalance), and it trends until it finds a new range to rotate in. Balance Imbalance Price rotates inside a range. Both sides agree on value. Value is no longer accepted. Price trends to a new range. breakout This is exactly what we're reading at every level: Price rejected at the edge Price accepted beyond it It can't build volume past the level, so it rotates Volume builds past the level, so the market wants back towards value. That's the Snap. new prices. That's the Flip, or the Magnet. KEY TA KEAWAY Every time price reaches a level, the question is the same: does the market accept it, or reject it? 4

VP ACADEMY #03 PA R T 0 2 Reading a Profile Volume at each price, turned sideways. A profile shows how much volume traded at each price. Long bars are prices the market liked. Short bars are prices it passed through. HVN LVN VAH Top edge of value POC Busiest price VAL Bottom edge of value 70% of vol. POC POINT OF CONTROL VAH and VAL VALUE AREA HIGH / LOW The price with the most volume: the fairest price of that The top and bottom of the 70% of volume. The edges of session. value. In our levels: NYVAH/NYVAL, ONVAH/ONVAL, PWVAH/PWVAL, dVAH/dVAL. HVN HIGH VOLUME NODE LVN LOW VOLUME NODE A thick bulge of volume. Price slows down and gets stuck there. A thin gap. Price was rejected there, so it moves through fast. Counts as a confluence, and a warning if it builds just above or below your level. Why price can fly from one level to the next. 5

VP ACADEMY #03 PA R T 0 2 Expensive, Fair and Cheap Your developing profile splits the day into three zones. Remember the durian stall: too expensive, fair, too cheap. The developing profile shows you exactly where those zones are today. EXPENSIVE Above the dVAH: buyers are paying up dVAH dPOC FA I R VA LU E Between dVAH and dVAL: where today's business is done dVAL CHEAP Below the dVAL: sellers are giving it away When price pushes above the dVAH or below the dVAL, it's testing whether the market will accept those prices. One of two things happens: It snaps straight back Volume builds out there Price goes into expensive or cheap and buyers or sellers step in immediately. The market doesn't want those prices. The Magnet is not valid here. Price stays and volume builds above the dVAH or below the dVAL. The market likes these prices. Now the dPOC retest is a Magnet, continuing the way price broke. KEY TA KEAWAY Above the dVAH is expensive, below the dVAL is cheap. What matters is whether the market accepts it. 6

VP ACADEMY #03 PA R T 0 3 Stacking Levels into a Grade More levels in one place, stronger reaction. One level on its own can work. But when several levels land at the same price, a lot more orders are waiting there, so the reaction is usually stronger. That's what our grade measures. 3 levels stacked together = 3 confluences = A grade ONVAH PWPOC VWAP band A NYVAL C 1 level on its own = 1 confluence = C grade GRADE CONFLUENCES WHAT COUNTS S 4 or more Any VAH, POC or VAL from the NY, overnight, weekly or developing profile, plus VWAP or a A 3 B 2 C 1 VWAP band, plus an HVN. KEY TA KEAWAY Count the levels sitting together. The more there are, the higher the grade. 8

pages: PROFILE SHAPES Read the shape, pick the setup VP ACADEMY · 04

VP ACADEMY #04 S TA RTHERE One idea Where the volume built tells you who won. The shape tells you who's in control. In Volume Profile 101 you learned that volume builds where the market accepts a price. Step back and look at where it built across the whole profile, and you get its shape. A fat middle means both sides agreed. Volume piled up at the top or bottom means one side won. A long, thin profile means one side was in control all day. D P b Trend Balance Buyers won Sellers won One side all day DURING YOUR SESSION Watch the developing profile take shape. It tells you whether to keep fading the edges or switch to trading the breakout. 2

VP ACADEMY #04 SHAPE 01 The D-Shape Balance. My favourite to trade. Fat in the middle, thin at both ends, with the POC near the centre. Buyers and sellers agree on value, so price keeps rotating inside the range instead of going anywhere. Accepted above: fades now lower probability short short VAH POC long How we trade it: the Snap 🫰 long VAL When the odds change Short at the VAH, where it's expensive. Long at the Price ranges just above the VAH or just below the VAL, where it's cheap. Target back towards value. VAL, and an HVN starts building there. The market is accepting new prices, so the balance is over. Then do it again. You can ping pong VAH to VAL for as long as the edges keep holding. From here, fades are lower probability and the Flip is higher probability. KEY TA KEAWAY Balance means fade the edges. Keep fading until the market accepts a price outside them. 3

VP ACADEMY #04 SHAPES 02 & 03 The P and b Shapes One side won, then the market settled. These two are mirror images. Price moved hard one way and left a thin tail behind it, then stopped and built value at the new prices. The fat part is where the market settled. The thin tail is where it moved through fast. If price pushes above the VAH and is accepted in the thin tail, Flip long on the retest. KEY TA KEAWAY Trading with the side that built the value is higher probability. Fading against it is lower. 4

guides.title: #05 Why the Setups Work
guides.line: The auction behind the Snap, the Flip and the Magnet.
pages: WHY THE SETUPS WORK The auction behind the Snap, the Flip and the Magnet VP ACADEMY · 05

VP ACADEMY #05 S TA RTHERE One Question Every setup is an answer to it. Does the market accept this price, or reject it? Every time price reaches a level, the auction has to decide. Either it builds volume there and keeps going, or it can't, and it turns around. The Snap, the Flip and the Magnet aren't three separate strategies. They're the three ways that question gets answered, and each one puts you on the side of the answer. Price reaches a level Accept it, or reject it? Rejected Accepted Accepted past the dVAH/L No volume builds past it Volume builds beyond it Then back to fair value Fade it back to value Trade the retest 🫰 The Snap 🔄 The Flip KEY TA KEAWAY Read the answer first. The answer tells you the setup. 2 🧲 The Magnet Trade the dPOC retest

VP ACADEMY #05 SETUP 01 Why the Snap Works Rejection. Price runs out of fuel at the level. Level Can't build volume past it Nobody left to push it further Rotates back to value Stretched away from value Thin past the level VALUE 1 The level has memory. It's a price the market already did business at, so orders are resting there waiting for price to come back. 2 Price arrives stretched. By the time it reaches a level, it's usually moved away from value into expensive or cheap prices. 3 Nobody is left to push it. If the auction can't build volume past the level, there's no one willing to keep trading at those prices. With no fuel, price rotates back to value. WHYS TA CKEDLEVELSARESTRONGER Every level you stack adds more resting orders at the same price. That's why an A or S grade Snap is higher probability than a lone C. WHENTHESNAPIS LO WERPROBABILI TY An HVN builds just above or below the level, price cuts through the dPOC with no reaction on the way there, or the dPOC sits just beyond the level. All three mean the market may be accepting new prices, not rejecting them. 3

VP ACADEMY #05 SETUP 02 Why the Flip Works Acceptance. The level switches sides. Volume builds beyond it Shorts sold the level here Now trapped below it Level The retest Old ceiling, new floor 1 The market accepted new prices. Price didn't just poke through the level. It built volume beyond it, which means the auction is happy doing business there. 2 The other side is trapped. Everyone who defended the level is now on the wrong side of it. When price comes back, they're looking to get out, and that adds fuel in your direction. 3 The retest is the best price. The move has already proven itself. The retest lets you join it at the level, with a tight stop on the other side. THE REINFORCED FLIP If an HVN built at the level before it broke, that volume becomes a wall behind the retest. It reinforces the level, which makes the Flip even higher probability. 4

VP ACADEMY #05 SETUP 03 Why the Magnet Works Acceptance, then back to fair value. Acceptance above the dVAH dVAH dPOC Back to fair value Continue the way it broke dVAL 1 The dPOC pulls price back. It's where the most business got done today, the fairest price of the session, so price keeps getting drawn back to it. 2 Acceptance shows the direction. When volume builds beyond the dVAH or dVAL, the market likes those new prices. Value is moving that way. 3 You enter at fair value. The pullback to the dPOC lets you join a direction the market has already chosen, at fair value instead of chasing it. WHENTHEM AG NETIS LO WERPROBABILI TY Price goes past the dVAH or dVAL and snaps straight back without building any volume out there. The market rejected those prices, so there's no direction to continue, and the dPOC is just the middle of the range. 5

VP ACADEMY #05 SUMMARY All Three on One Page One question, three answers. SETUP 🫰 Snap 🔄 Flip 🧲 Magnet THE MARKET'S ANSWER WHY IT WORKS Rejected at the level The level has memory, price is stretched, and nobody is left to push it further. Accepted beyond the level New prices are accepted, the defenders are trapped, and the retest is the best entry. Accepted past the dVAH/L, then back The dPOC pulls price back, and acceptance shows which way to continue. KEY TA KEAWAY You're never guessing. You're waiting for the market to answer, then trading with the answer. See every setup traded live in #setup-library. Education only, not financial advice. 6

guides.title: #06 VWAP and ATR
guides.line: VWAP bands as confluence, and ATR × 2 for your stop.
pages: V WA PAND AT R Fair value, stretch and stop size VP ACADEMY · 06

VP ACADEMY #06 PA R T 0 1 What VWAP Is The session's average price, weighted by volume. VWAP stands for volume-weighted average price. It takes every price traded this session and averages them, giving more weight to the prices where more volume traded. The result is one line: the average price everyone has paid today. VWAP Session starts (18:00 ET) → It resets every session (we anchor it to Session, so on CME futures it starts fresh at 18:00 ET) and moves with price as the day builds. VWAP POC The average price of the session, weighted by volume. A moving line that shifts with every trade. The single price with the most volume. A level that only moves when a new price becomes the busiest. SETTINGS RECAP Anchor Period: Session. Source: (H + L + C) / 3. Bands: Standard Deviation, multipliers 1, 2 and 3. Full walkthrough in VP Academy #01: Chart Setup. KEY TA KEAWAY Both measure fair value. The POC is where the most business got done. VWAP is the average price it got done at. 2

VP ACADEMY #06 PA R T 0 1 The Three Bands How stretched price is from fair value. Around VWAP we plot three bands on each side, at 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. In plain terms, a standard deviation is how far price usually wanders from VWAP this session. The bands are built from the session's own volatility, so they widen on busy days and tighten on quiet ones. Band 3 Band 2 VWAP Band 1 Band 2 Band 3 1 Inside band 1: price is close to the session's average. Normal rotation. 2 Out at band 2: price is stretched away from fair value. 3 Out at band 3: price is very stretched. It's travelled a long way from where the session's business has been done. Think of it like your developing profile VWAP Bands is like the dPOC: the centre of today's fair value. are like the dVAH and dVAL: the edges of value. Above the upper bands is expensive, below the lower bands is cheap. They're calculated differently, so they won't sit on the same prices. But they answer the same question: where is fair value, and how far has price stretched from it? 3 more stretched Band 1

VP ACADEMY #06 PA R T 0 1 How We Use VWAP A confluence, never a trade on its own. VWAP and the bands don't give us trades. Our levels do. VWAP's job is to make a level stronger when it lines up with one. VWAP Band 1 dVAL dVAL + Band 1 = 2 confluences B grade Snap Counts as a confluence Not a setup on its own VWAP or any of its bands sitting on your level adds one confluence to your grade. VWAP or a band with no level behind it is not a trade. Price is reaching your level and is stretched from the session average at the same time, so more traders are watching that price. No level, no setup. The bands only ever add to a level you already have marked. KEY TA KEAWAY VWAP adds to a level. It never replaces one. 4

VP ACADEMY #06 PA R T 0 2 What ATR Is How big a candle usually is right now. ATR stands for average true range. It measures how much price typically moves in one candle, including any gaps. We set it to 60 with RMA smoothing, so on the 1-minute chart it's roughly the average candle size over the last hour. The reading is in points, so ATR × 2 gives you your stop in points. Stop loss = ATR × 2 points Target = same distance 1:1 Your level Stop = ATR × 2 Room for the wick Wick through the level Stop still safe ATR tells you how much room a trade needs. Doubling it gives the trade room to breathe: if price wicks through your level before reacting, your stop is still outside the noise. With 1:1 targets, your target is the same distance the other way. VP ACADEMY #09 THE MINDSET A Business, Not a Bet How to think about prop firms before you buy a single evaluation. Most traders treat an evaluation like a lottery ticket: buy one, hope it passes, and feel crushed when it doesn't. Treat the prop firm game strictly as a business instead. You have a product that works, which is your edge, and prop firms let you put it to work on their capital. IN A BUSINESS IN YOUR PROP BUSINESS Your product Your edge: 3–4 setups a session, a 65–70% win rate and 1:1 targets. Startup costs Evaluation fees. Every business spends money before it makes money. Revenue Payouts from your funded accounts. Risk management Breakeven at 75%, a loss cap on every account, and sizing by stars. Bookkeeping The Prop Tracker: costs, drawdown floors and payouts, account by account. Scaling up Running 2–3 accounts at once, so none of your setups go to waste. KEY TA KEAWAYA business owner doesn't quit because one month had costs. Judge your prop business on the whole picture, not on one evaluation. 2

VP ACADEMY #09 THE MINDSET Why the ROI Is So High Small, fixed costs against a much bigger upside. In most businesses you need thousands to get started, and you can lose a lot more than you put in. With a prop firm, your cost is the evaluation fee. That's the most you can lose on an account, and a single payout can be many times that. EXAMPLE COST PAYOUT RETURN One evaluation passes and pays out $50 $1,000 20× your money You blow 3 evaluations for every 1 that pays $200 $1,000 5× your money Illustrative numbers only. Fees and payouts vary by firm and change often, so check the current prices and count every fee (evaluation, activation, resets) as a cost. Even when most evaluations fail, a business with costs this small and returns this big stays profitable. That's why the real question is never "did this one evaluation pass?" It's "am I net positive across all of them?" WHERETOS TA R T : APEX Apex is the cheapest option on the market and a good starter firm. Low evaluation fees keep your startup costs down while you get your first payouts. KEY TA KEAWAY Your downside per account is the fee. Your upside is every payout after it. 3

VP ACADEMY #09 THE SETUP Choosing Your Account Size Pick the account that gives you the most room for the least work. Every account size comes with two numbers: the profit target you have to hit, and the drawdown you're allowed to lose. What matters isn't how big the account is, but how those two compare. The ratio to check My recommendation: 50K Profit target ÷ drawdown. The 50K account has the best profit target to drawdown ratio, so that's the size I recommend. The lower the number, the less profit you have to make for every dollar of room you're given. That makes the account easier to pass with the same edge. It's also cheaper, which keeps your startup costs low while you build up to 2–3 accounts. COM PA REBEFOREYOUBUY Firms change their targets, drawdowns and prices often. Before you buy, check the current numbers for each size and work out the ratio yourself. The Prop Firm Hacking Tool then shows you the risk per trade and contract size for the account you choose. KEEP YO URRE CO RDSINTHEPROPT RAC KERA business keeps its books. Log every evaluation fee, activation fee and payout, and each account's drawdown floor, in the Prop Tracker. Then you always know your real net across all your accounts, not just how today went. VP ACADEMY #09 THE RULES Intraday vs EOD Trailing The two ways a trailing drawdown can follow you. Intraday trailing End-of-day (EOD) trailing Your drawdown floor follows your highest balance Your drawdown floor only moves at the end of the in real time, including open profit while you're still in a trade. day, based on your closing balance. What happens inside a trade during the day doesn't move it. If a trade runs into profit and then comes back, the floor has already moved up and stays there. INTRADAY TRAILING END-OF-DAY (EOD) TRAILING Your balance Your balance Drawdown floor Drawdown floor Day 1 Day 2 Day 1 The floor follows every new high, even open profit inside a trade. Day 2 The floor only moves at the close, based on your closing balance. WHY WE USE INTRADAY TRAILING Intraday trailing is much cheaper than EOD. And it doesn't affect us much, because we're strictly taking small 1:1 moves: we're in and out quickly and don't sit in big open profits for the floor to chase. Breakeven at 75% (next page) covers the rest. Many firms stop trailing once the floor reaches your starting balance. Rules differ by firm and by account type, so always read yours. 5

VP ACADEMY #09 THE RULES Protecting Every Account Three rules, on every account, every session. 1 Breakeven at 75% Once price is 75% of the way to your target, move your stop to breakeven. On an intraday trail, a winner that comes all the way back would leave you with a loss and a higher floor. Breakeven at 75% is what protects you from the trail. 2 A 1–2 loss cap per account, per session That's your risk management. Once an account takes its 1 or 2 losses for the session, it's done until the next one. No revenge trades, and no single bad session can take an account out. 3 Size by stars, never by your last result 1★ is 1 contract, 2★ is 2 contracts, and 3★ is 2–3 contracts. Use the Prop Firm Hacking Tool to work out the right risk per trade for your account's rules before you start. The loss cap protects you from yourself. 6

VP ACADEMY #09 GETTING PA I D From Passed to Payout What happens after you pass, using an Apex 50K account as the example. 1 Pay the activation fee Passing the evaluation isn't the last cost. Most firms charge an activation fee to turn a passed account into a funded one. Count it as a startup cost in your books, just like the evaluation fee. 2 Follow the consistency rule Once you're funded, a consistency rule applies: no single day can make up too big a share of your profit. Our small, steady 1:1 trades fit this naturally. One huge day can actually hold up your payout. 3 Hit 5 winning days You need a minimum of 5 winning days before you can request a payout. 4 Get above $52,100 for your first payout On a 50K account, your balance must be above $52,100 before your first payout. From there you can request as little as $500. EVERY PA YOUTAFTERTHEFIRSTISEASIER The first payout is the hardest, because you have to build that buffer above $52,100 first. Once it's built, each payout after that only needs the winning days and the profit to withdraw, so they come much more easily. These are Apex's rules for a 50K account as I trade it. Firms change their rules often, so always check the current ones for your firm and account size. KEY TA KEAWAY Pass, activate, build the buffer once, and then the payouts get easier. 7

VP ACADEMY #09 SCALING UP Run 2–3 Accounts Don't let your edge go to waste. We get a lot of setups every day. With only one account, the loss cap ends your session early and every setup after that goes to waste. I recommend running 2–3 accounts at once, so you can keep taking advantage of your edge. CONCENTRATED: ONE ACCOUNT AT A TIME Account AWLL Account B Account C Loss cap hit: switch W W Still under its cap Ready if B hits its cap Trade one account at a time. When it hits its loss cap, move to the next. Don't copy-trade Why it works Copying the same entry onto every account means one loss hits all of them at once. Instead, spread your trades across accounts with one of the two models on the next page. Your edge plays out over many trades. More accounts means more of your setups actually get taken, and one bad stretch on a single account doesn't stop the business. KEY TA KEAWAY Your edge only makes money on the setups you actually take. More accounts, more setups taken. 8

VP ACADEMY #09 SCALING UP Concentrated vs Round Robin Two ways to spread your trades across accounts. Concentrated Round robin Trade one account until it hits its loss cap, then Each trade goes on the next account in turn: A, then switch to the next (the diagram on the previous page). B, then C, then back to A. Pros: your wins stack on one account, so it reaches Pros: wins and losses are spread across every account, so each one swings much less. Lower the profit target faster. variance. Cons: a losing streak lands on one account, so that account swings much more and is more likely to Cons: each account moves towards its target more slowly. blow. ROUND ROBIN: EACH TRADE GOES ON THE NEXT ACCOUNT Account A Account BWLLW Account CWW ACCOUNT HOW TO RUN IT Evaluations Concentrated. The job is to pass, so let your wins stack and get through quickly. A blown evaluation is a startup cost. Funded accounts Round robin, and play it more conservatively. These are your revenue, so protect them. Rotating between accounts reduces the variance on each one. KEY TA KEAWAY Evaluations: concentrated, to pass fast. Funded accounts: round robin and more conservative, to protect your payouts. 9

VP ACADEMY #09 THEMIS TA KES The Biggest Mistakes I See And how a business owner would think about them instead. Trading evaluations too conservatively Getting attached to one evaluation Tiny size makes an evaluation drag on for weeks, One account is not your business. When you treat a and you pay for that time while your edge sits unused. An evaluation is there to be passed. Size by stars as normal, and use the Hacking Tool to find a single evaluation as everything, you start trading scared, and that's when the mistakes come. size that passes efficiently. Blowing accounts is normal, as long as you're net positive. Here's what a good month can look like, even with half the accounts blown: EXAMPLE MONTH AMOUNT 4 evaluations bought −$200 2 of them blown $0 Activation fee for the passed account −$100 1 payout from that account +$1,000 Net for the month +$700 Illustrative numbers only. Track your real costs and payouts in the Prop Tracker. THE RIGHT MINDSET Treat a blown account as a business expense. It's just the cost of doing business. Prop firm accounts aren't meant to be there forever: that's how they're designed. Your job isn't to keep one account alive. It's to stay net positive across all of them. KEY TA KEAWAY Blown accounts are a cost of doing business. Net positive across all your accounts is the only number that matters. Education only, not financial advice. Trading futures, on your own capital or a prop firm's, involves risk. 10

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC REASON 01 Real data, not drawn patterns Every level I trade comes from where volume actually traded. Before I traded volume profile, I traded ICT and smart money concepts on forex. EUR/USD, GBP/JPY and gold, in the London Open Killzone, with three trade models and a long confluence checklist of nonnegotiables. I took it seriously, and I put real hours into it. At its core, ICT is pattern trading. Order blocks, fair value gaps, breakers and market structure shifts are all shapes drawn from candles. But the market doesn't move because of a candlestick pattern, and there's no hidden algorithm reading the gap between two wicks. Price moves because buyers and sellers are auctioning to find fair value. What changed everything for me was switching to volume profile trading. Instead of drawing patterns and guessing what they meant, I could finally see the auction itself: where contracts actually traded, where the market found fair value, and where it rejected price. Every level on my chart now comes from real transactions, not from my read of a candle. Once I saw that, it was very hard to go back to drawing boxes and gaps. ICT tells you a story about where price should go. Volume profile shows you where the market actually traded. PAT TERNTRADINGVSAUCTIONTRADINGICT / SMC ( WHEREIS TA RTED ) VOLUMEPROFILE ( W H AT ITRADENOW ) ✕ Levels drawn from candle patterns: order blocks, ✓ Levels built from real traded volume: VAH, POC ✕ Bias built on a story about where price "should" ✓ Trades where price is relative to value, nothing ✕ Needs a trend and displacement for the patterns ✓ Works in ranges, breakouts and trends ✓ Everyone gets the same levels, so the read is gaps, breakers and VAL go more to work ✕ Two traders can read the same chart completely objective differently TRY THIS Pull up yesterday's chart and mark it two ways. First, your ICT levels: the order blocks and fair value gaps you'd normally draw. Then put a session profile on and mark the VAH, POC and VAL. Watch today's session and see which levels price actually respects. Do it for a week, and the data will make the argument for me. 2

When to trade Killzones, with the best setups mostly in one or two windows Every session builds its own profile, so Asia, London and NY all have levels Why price moves A narrative about an algorithm delivering price Auction market theory: a two-sided auction looking for fair value PREMIUM , FAIRVALUEANDDISCOUNT, FROMREALVOLUME VAH · premium The top of value, where 70% of volume ends above POC · fair value The single price with the most contracts traded VAL · discount The bottom of value, where 70% of volume ends below No ranges to choose and no Fibonacci tool. The profile works out premium, fair value and discount from the contracts that actually traded. The way I see it: as long as I have the profile on my chart and my value levels marked, I don't need a single candlestick pattern. I trade where price is relative to value, and that's it. 3

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC REASON 02 Any market condition No more waiting for the "right" kind of market. Spend any time around ICT and SMC traders and you'll hear the same complaints. "Price action is too choppy." "This month is lower probability because of the holidays, the news, the range." "You need the market to trend to make money, you can't do much in a range." That's not bad luck. It's built into the method. Pattern trading needs displacement and a clean trend to work, so when the market rotates sideways, which it does a lot of the time, the patterns stop working and you're told to sit on your hands for weeks. With volume profile, a range isn't a problem. It's a setup. EVERY KIND OF DAY HAS A PLAY WHAT THE MARKET IS DOING WHAT ICT TENDS TO SAY WHAT I TRADE Balanced, rotating day (Dshape) "Choppy. Lower probability. Wait for a cleaner day." The Snap : fade the VAH and VAL and ping-pong between them until price breaks out of value. This is my favourite day to trade. Breaking out of value Wait for a sweep, a shift and a return to an order block The Flip : once price accepts beyond a level, trade the retest of it from the other side Trending day (P or b-shape) The one condition where the patterns work best The Magnet back to the dPOC for continuation, or The Wall off an HVN shelf when there are no levels left Fake breakout that snaps back "Liquidity sweep", usually spotted after the fact The Whip : price breaks dVAH or dVAL with no volume and whips straight back into value No level in play Hunt for a pattern somewhere on the chart No trade. No level means no edge, so I wait for price to come to one 🫰 🔄 🧲 🧱 ⚡ The point: I don't need the market to behave a certain way. Whatever it does, the profile tells me where value is, and my setups tell me how to trade around it. There's no such thing as a "bad month" for the method, only for my discipline. 4

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC REASON 03 Small moves, all day long Scalping what's there, instead of waiting for the big one. From my experience, ICT and SMC need a long chain of things to happen before you're allowed to take a trade. You wait for the right session, a liquidity sweep, a market structure shift, a displacement leg, a gap to form, then price to return to it. When it all finally lines up, you're aiming for one big move. And that doesn't happen often. I scalp. I take small moves, level to level, with a 1:1 target. Those small reactions happen over and over again, every single day, in every session. A reaction of a few points off a real volume level happens many times a day. A huge trend leg doesn't. 2 They work in any session. I live in Singapore, so I can trade the Asia session properly, not just stay up for New York. 3 They're easier to repeat. Same levels, same setups, same 1:1 target, every day. That's what builds consistency, and consistency is what gets you funded. 5

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC REASON 04 Confidence and clarity No more confluences fighting each other. The overnight POC, the New York POC and the VWAP band all sat in the same small zone. Three confluences, stacked. That's a 3-star Snap. 2 One plan, no conflict Sell at the ONPOC, with the stop above the NYPOC plus a buffer. Every confluence agreed: this was value, and price was coming up into it. 3 The market did its thing Price pushed into the NYPOC, reacted and rolled over to the downside. Target hit, +1R. 4 No second-guessing No pattern to interpret and no story to believe. Just price coming back to where the market had already done the most business. 6

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC REASON 05 The market isn't a puzzle The most damaging idea I unlearned. The way ICT is taught makes the market feel solvable. There's always another concept to learn, another PDA you didn't spot, another gap at another Fibonacci level. Lose a trade, and the answer is always that you missed something. That mindset is brutal for traders. It turns every loss into a personal failure and sends you down an endless rabbit hole looking for the one secret that makes losses stop. That secret doesn't exist. You can't solve the market. You can only make good bets, manage your risk, and let the numbers play out. Volume profile changed how I think about this. I know I'm trading a real, data-backed edge, and I also accept that the market has a huge amount of randomness in it. I can have every confluence lined up and still be wrong. That doesn't mean I missed something. It means that trade was one of the losers that every edge has. 3–4 65–70% 1:1 setups per session win rate on my system risk to reward With numbers like these, roughly one trade in three will lose, and that's built into the plan. My job isn't to avoid losses. It's to take every valid setup, size it properly, and let the edge work over hundreds of trades. AFTERA LO SS , THEI CT QUE ST IONAFTERA LO SS , MYQUE ST IONNOW ✕ "What did I miss?" ✓ "Was it a valid setup at my level?" ✓ "Did I size it by the stars and respect my stop?" ✓ If yes to both, move on to the next setup. ✕ "Which concept do I need to learn next?" ✕ "Maybe I need a new model." REFLECT, DON ' TOBSESS It's still worth reviewing your losses, which is exactly what the weekly self review is for. The question is "did I follow my process?", not "what secret did I miss?". If you followed the plan, a loss is just the cost of doing business. 7

WHY I LEFT ICT/SMC THEB OT TOM LINE Why I'm not going back Five reasons, one conclusion. 1 Real data, not drawn patterns. My levels come from where contracts actually traded, not from shapes on candles. 2 Any market condition. Ranges, breakouts and trends each have a setup, so I'm never waiting for the right kind of month. 3 Small moves, all day long. I scalp 1:1 reactions that happen in every session, instead of waiting days for one big move. 4 Confidence and clarity. My confluences stack instead of clash, so I execute without second-guessing. 5 The market isn't a puzzle. I trade an edge and accept that losses are part of it, instead of hunting for a secret. TO B E FA I R Volume profile isn't magic. You'll still lose trades, you still need risk rules, and you still need the discipline to wait for your levels. It won't fix overtrading or revenge trading on its own. What it gives you is a clear, objective edge built on real data, so the only thing left to work on is you. THE BOTTOM LINE I switched because I wanted to trade what the market is actually doing, not what a pattern says it should do. That one change gave me clarity, confidence and a much healthier relationship with losing. WHERE TO S TA R T VP Academy #03 · Volume Profile 101 How the auction works, and why our levels matter. BASE HITS WHY I SCALP Base Hits, Not Home Runs The goal is the reaction at the level, not the whole move. When you start trading, everyone tells you scalping is gambling. Hold for the big move, they say, and go for 1:3 or more. If you came from ICT or SMC like I did, that's exactly what you were taught. This framework does the opposite. Our objective is to capture small moves: base hits. Every trade I take targets 1:1. I'm not trying to catch the whole move. I'm trying to catch the reaction at a level, because that's the part of the move that's most likely to happen. Think about how often each one actually shows up. Big moves are rare. You might get a handful a week, and you won't catch all of them. Small moves happen every single day, at level after level, session after session. If you're only hunting the big move, you'll get far less of it than the small moves I'm taking every day. WHY I TRADE THIS WAY 1 It's simple probability. A small move is far more likely to happen than a big one. 2 It's a smoother ride. The same edge, with much shorter losing streaks and smaller drawdowns. 3 It keeps my head right. Winning often keeps me confident, and stops fear from wrecking my execution. KEY TA KEAWAY Base hits win the game. I don't need the market to give me everything. I just need it to give me the reaction, every day. 2

BASE HITS PA R T 0 1 Simple Probability Ask the market for less, and it says yes more often. You're long at a level with your stop below. What's more likely: price moving up 1R to a 1:1 target, or 3R to a 1:3 target? Common sense answers that one. The 1:1 gets hit far more often. 1:3 TARGET 1:3 never comes 1:1 hit, I'm out 1:1 TARGET ✓ ENTRY AT THE LEVEL STOP The 1:3 trader is stopped out or at breakeven This is the trade every 1:3 trader knows. Price reacts off the level and runs straight past 1:1. You think you're in a winner. Then it rolls over, and you either get stopped out or you're back at breakeven, after the market had already paid you. I took the 1:1 and I'm out. A 1:3 needs you to be right about the direction, the distance and the timing. A 1:1 only needs the reaction. Small reactions happen at good levels all the time, even against the trend, so I can be wrong about where the market is going for the day and still get paid at the level. KEY TA KEAWAYA 1:1 asks the market for the reaction. A 1:3 asks it to be right about everything else too. 3

BASE HITS PA R T 0 2 Same Edge, Different Ride On paper the two can make the same money. Living through them is another story. “But you make less money on a 1:1.” Not necessarily. Compare my numbers with an example 1:3 trader who wins 35% of the time. Both make +0.4R per trade on average. Same edge on paper. Now look at what it feels like to trade each one. 1:1 at 70% 1:3 at 35% How I trade Example trader Average edge per trade +0.4R 3 Typical longest losing streak in 100 trades Typical biggest drawdown in 100 trades Chance of 5+ losses in a row in 100 trades Average edge per trade Typical longest losing streak in 100 trades 4R Typical biggest drawdown in 100 trades 15% Chance of 5+ losses in a row in 100 trades +0.4R 9 10R 99% I simulated 40,000 runs of 100 trades for each trader. The figures are the typical (median) result. Nine losses in a row and a 10R drawdown, just as normal variance. On a prop account with a tight drawdown, that alone can end the account before the edge ever shows up. And which trader do you think is still following their rules on loss number eight? WANTMOREMONEY ? ADDSIZE , NOTDIS TA NCE Any move can pay well if your size is right. A small, reliable move with the right size beats a big move you only catch some of the time. Size comes from the setup's grade and your account, not from stretching the target. 4

BASE HITS PA R T 0 3 Built for Prop Accounts Same edge on paper. Only one of them survives a trailing drawdown. Here are those two traders as equity curves: one run of 100 trades each, both ending at +40R. The 1:1 climbs in a steady staircase. The 1:3 gets there through long losing stretches and deep drawdowns. 1:1 at 70% +40R never more than 3R down Prop account blown at trade 4 4% trailing drawdown hit at 1% risk per trade +30R 1:3 at 35% +20R +10R 0 −10R drawdown -10R 19 trades to get back to the high 0 25 50 75 TRADES 100 The 1:3 ends up in the same place, but goes nowhere for 35 trades and has a 10R drawdown. On a prop account, you don't get to sit through that. With a 4% trailing drawdown, the account was gone at trade 4. 1:1 at 70% 1:3 at 35% 6% target · 4% trailing DD · 1% risk Same eval, same edge Evals passed 89% Evals passed 53% Accounts blown 11% Accounts blown 47% Typical trades to pass 12 Typical trades to pass The 1:3 run in the chart is a typical one, with the usual 10R drawdown. Eval figures are from 40,000 simulated evals each. The 1:3 passes quicker when it passes, but it blows almost half its accounts. KEY TA KEAWAY Props don't pay for the size of your wins. They pay you for staying inside the drawdown. 1:1 is built for exactly that. 5 5

BASE HITS PA R T 0 4 · PA YOUTRULES The Consistency Rule Big wins can actually stop you getting paid. Many prop firms have a consistency rule: before they pay you out, no single day can make up more than a set share of your total profit, usually 30% to 50%. That share is your consistency score: best day ÷ total profit. HOW IT WORKS You've made $3,000 in total and your best day was $1,500. That's $1,500 ÷ $3,000 = 50%. If your firm's rule is 30%, you can't take a payout yet. You have to keep trading until your total reaches $5,000, just so that one big day drops to 30%. The big day didn't get you paid faster. It delayed your payout. With 1:3, one winning trade is +3R, so a couple of wins in a day gives you a huge day, with red days in between. Your profit comes in lumps. With 1:1, a great day is a few R, and profit builds in small, even steps. 1:1 · 10 trading days 1:3 · 10 trading days +5 +3 +1 +3 +1 +5 +3 +1 +1 -1 +5 +1 +1 +1 +1 +1 -1 -3 Total profit +12R · best day +3R -3 -3 Total profit +10R · best day +5R Best day = 25% of profit ✓ passes a 30% rule Best day = 50% of profit ✗ fails a 30% rule MEE TS A 3 0 % CO NSI ST E N CY RULE 1 : 1 AT 7 0 % 1 : 3 AT 3 5 % After 10 trading days 74% 19% After 20 trading days 98% 47% 3 trades a day, 40,000 simulated runs each. Every firm sets its own rule, so check yours before you trade the account. KEY TA KEAWAY Firms want steady profit, not one lucky day. 1:1 gives them exactly that. 6

BASE HITS PA R T 0 4 · PA YOUTRULES The Winning Days Rule Payouts need green days, and 1:1 gives you more of them. Most firms also want a minimum number of winning days before they pay you out, often 5. A winning day is simply a day that closes in profit, usually above a small minimum. With 3–4 trades a day, a 1:1 day finishes green about 7 days in 10, so 5 winning days come quickly. High R traders usually don't take many trades. They wait for the perfect setup: maybe one trade a day, often only 2–3 a week. With one trade, a day is only green if that one trade wins, and at a 35% win rate most days aren't. On days with no setup at all, there's no chance of a winning day. WINNING DAYS 1 : 1 AT 7 0 % 1 : 3 AT 3 5 % 1 : 3 AT 3 5 % 3–4 trades a day 1 trade a day 2–3 trades a week 72% 35% 18% 7 14 27 69% 5% <1% Days that finish green Typical trading days to get 5 winning days 5 winning days within your first 7 trading days 40,000 simulated runs each. A winning day here is any day that closes at +1R or more. That's 7 trading days for me, against nearly 3 weeks for the high R trader taking one trade a day, and 5– 6 weeks if they only trade 2–3 times a week. PUT THE TWO RULES TOGETHER The 1:1 trader stacks up green days quickly, and no single day stands out, so both rules are usually met at the same time. The 1:3 trader is often still waiting on winning days, and even when they get there, one big day can push them over the consistency limit. That means more days of trading before they can get paid. KEY TA KEAWAY Steady green days tick every box a prop firm checks. Lumpy days often don't. 7

BASE HITS PA R T 0 5 Less Time In, Less Randomness Why scalping is actually the lower-risk way to trade. People think holding for the big move is the safe, professional way, and that scalping is the risky one. It's the other way round. The market isn't pre-programmed to go to your target. Nobody can predict exactly where it's going. W H AT SCALPINGGIVESYOU 1 Less exposure. The longer you hold, the more you're exposed to random spikes, news and reversals. A scalp takes the reaction and gets out. Less time in the trade means less left to luck. 2 More reps. With 3–4 setups a session, I'm executing the same thing over and over instead of waiting days for one perfect trade. That's how execution gets sharp, and it gives you far more trades to review. 3 Smaller swings. Smaller targets mean smaller stops and smaller P&L swings. Each trade matters less on its own, so there's less emotion riding on it. Taking a trade becomes routine. 4 No trade carries the day. When your one trade of the day has everything riding on it, every tick hurts. When it's one of many, you can let the numbers play out. Your edge only shows up over a big sample An edge doesn't pay you trade by trade. It shows up over a hundred trades or more. If you're waiting for the big move, you can sit there for days without a valid setup, and your edge plays out painfully slowly. With 3–4 setups a session, I get through that sample in weeks, not months. KEY TA KEAWAY Scalping isn't gambling. Holding and hoping for 3R is the bigger bet. I take what the level gives me and get out. 8

BASE HITS PA R T 0 6 The Winner Effect Why your win rate changes how well you trade. There's an idea in trading psychology called the winner effect. When you win consistently, your confidence builds and you trade from a calm, clear head. The opposite is the loser effect: repeated losses push your stress up, and stress makes you timid. You start seeing every pullback as a threat. This is where 1:3 trading breaks down for most people. The maths only works if you let every trade run all the way to 3R. But after a string of losses, a normal pullback feels like a reversal. Trading for 1:3 Trading for 1:1 Price passes 1R, then pulls back. Fear kicks in. You move your stop to breakeven and get wicked out, or you close early on one red candle. Every early exit Price reaches 1R and the trade is done. Stop at breakeven once price is 75% of the way there. No decisions under pressure, no second-guessing. eats into the edge the 1:3 was supposed to give you. Winning most trades keeps you out of the loser effect. It's not about winning every day. It's about staying out of the loser effect, because that's where the tilt, the revenge trades and the blown accounts come from. KEY TA KEAWAYA high win rate isn't just a number. It keeps your head in the right place to keep executing properly. 9

BASE HITS PA R T 0 7 Not Any 1:1 A small target only works at the right price. None of this means you can take 1:1 trades anywhere. A 1:1 at a random price is a coin flip. The edge comes from taking it where a reaction is more likely than not: a weighted coin. That's what our levels are for. A marked level with volume behind it, read in the context of the developing profile, is where the auction is most likely to react. That's where I put my 1:1. HOWI TA KEEVE RY T RA D E 1 Only at a level. A valid Snap, Flip or Magnet at a marked level, with the developing profile as context. 2 Limit order. At the level for a Snap, on the retest for a Flip or a Magnet. 3 Target 1:1. I take the reaction, not the whole move. 4 Breakeven at 75%. Once price is three quarters of the way to target, the stop goes to breakeven. 5 3–4 setups a session. Base hits, repeated, every session. KEY TA KEAWAY Small target. High probability. Repeated every session. That's the whole game. 10

guides.title: Core Setups
guides.line: The Snap, the Flip and the Magnet.
pages: CORE SETUPS The Snap · The Flip · The Magnet

CORE SETUPS SETUP 01 The Snap Fading the level, back towards value. My most common setup, basically taking the fade of a level. WHY IT WORKS A level is a price the market has already done business at, so orders rest there and it carries a memory of value. Price normally arrives at one stretched away from value, and if the auction can’t build volume past it, there is nobody left to push it further. The fade is a bet that the level holds and price rotates back to value. OPPOSITE SIDE EXAMPLE 2

CORE SETUPS SETUP 02 The Flip The flipside retest of a broken level. Basically taking the flipside retest of a level that has been broken past. WHY IT WORKS When a level breaks and volume builds beyond it, the auction has accepted the new area and the side defending that level is now trapped on the wrong side of it. The level flips roles, and the retest is the cheapest entry into the move that has already proven itself. OPPOSITE SIDE EXAMPLE 3

CORE SETUPS SETUP 03 The Magnet The dPOC retest, back to fair value. This is my least common setup and has a very specific use case. It’s called The Magnet because we are taking a retest of the dPOC, and the dPOC is a magnet for price. We only take this setup when price has gone past the dVAL/H and comes back to the dPOC for a continuation trade. WHY IT WORKS The dPOC is the price the most business got done at, so it pulls price back to it. Once price has left the value area, that pull gives you a retest at fair value, and you take the continuation in the direction price already broke away. OPPOSITE SIDE EXAMPLE 4

guides.title: Bonus Tips
guides.line: Five scenarios to watch for.
pages: BONUS TIPS Five scenarios to watch for

BONUS TIPS SCENARIO 01 Two Levels, Close Together When there are 2 VP levels at a relatively close distance from one another. When you see 2 or 3 VP levels at a relatively close distance from one another, be cautious when trading them. More often than not, price tends to range in between these 2 lines, as both lines are significant, so price can’t decide between the 2 and tends to form a range. I would personally avoid trading in this scenario, as I’ll more likely be caught up in the chop and we DON’T want that. This situation, however, is completely different when the 2 or 3 VP levels are very close together. These are very high probability to trade and I would take these any day of the week. 2

BONUS TIPS SCENARIO 02 Volume Building at the Level When is it low probability to take the Snap. There is only 1 scenario where I will avoid taking the Snap, and it’s this particular scenario. When price starts ranging right above or below the level and builds a lot of volume in the profile (as seen by an HVN forming above or below the level). Think of the HVN forming as pressure and think of the level as a ceiling: what happens when there is a lot of pressure building on a ceiling? Yes, it’ll more than likely break. So that’s why I avoid the Snap in these situations, as it’ll more likely than not break through the level. Don’t worry though. When price breaks through the level and comes back for the retest, that’s what I call the Reinforced Flip, and that’s one of my highest probability setups. The HVN in this case will act as a defensive WALL for price, so it’ll essentially reinforce the level, making it stronger. In turn, this makes our flipside short even higher probability. 3

BONUS TIPS SCENARIO 03 Cutting Through the dPOC When price cuts through the dPOC with no reaction. In situations where you are looking to take a Snap off a level, and before reaching the level price impulsively cuts through the dPOC, that is a massive red flag and you should AVOID the Snap. This is because the dPOC is the place with the highest volume within the profile, and if price can easily cut through it with no reaction, it means price is actively seeking new fair value. So it’s very low probability to take a fade in the opposite direction in this case. 4

BONUS TIPS SCENARIO 04 Snapping Back from the dVAH/L When price snaps back down fast after going past the dVAH/L. When looking to take The Magnet setup, always avoid the setup when price goes beyond the dVAH/L and instantly snaps back down without building acceptance beyond the level. This just means that price went to the expensive/cheap region (the area above the dVAH/L) and buyers/sellers intercepted, so The Magnet is not valid here. Instead, you should only be taking The Magnet setup in this specific scenario: when price goes beyond the dVAH/L and builds acceptance beyond the level (you can see volume building beyond the dVAH/L). This means that price likes the expensive/cheap prices, and therefore it’s a higher probability retest when price comes back to the dPOC, as price would more likely want to continue in the same direction. 5

BONUS TIPS SCENARIO 05 The dPOC Just Above the Level When the dPOC sits right above or below the level. In the case where the dPOC is right above or below a VP level, you have to take into account that price might just go for the dPOC instead of reacting to the level below, as the dPOC acts as a STRONG magnet for price. Therefore, in these cases you might not want to take the Snap off the level if the dPOC is just above or below. Of course the trade can still play out, but it’s just a risk you have to keep in mind. 6

Read that first, and most of these mistakes disappear. 5

CO MMONMIS TA KES PA R T 0 2 Execution A good read, let down by the orders. 08 Stop too tight You use a small stop on gold or oil because it feels safer, and get wicked out just before price reacts. THEMI STA K E ✗ THE FIX ✓ 1:1 Level Level tight stop ATR × 2 stopped out WHYIT CO STS YO U THE FIX GC and CL often wick through a level before reacting. A tight stop is inside the noise, so you're right on direction and still lose. Use ATR × 2 points on gold and oil, read at the moment you place the order. It gives the trade room to breathe. See: VP Academy #06 and #07 09 Moving the stop or target Price comes towards your stop, so you widen it. Or price is in profit, so you close early before 1:1. Closing early cuts your winners below your losers, and a 65–70% win rate stops being enough. Set the stop and target when you place the order. The only adjustment is moving your stop to breakeven at 75% of the way to your target. See: VP Academy #07: Execution 6

CO MMONMIS TA KES PA R T 0 3 Discipline The mistakes that have nothing to do with the chart. 10 Not marking levels before the session The session starts and you're still drawing profiles, setting VWAP and finding ATR while price is moving. A bad day becomes a blown account. Two losses and you're done on that account for the day. The next session is a clean slate. If it's getting to you, open the Mindset tool. CO MMONMIS TA KES PA R T 0 3 Discipline The mistakes that have nothing to do with the chart. 12 Oversizing After a loss, you size up on the next trade to make it back faster, whatever the setup looks like. guides.title: Volume, Not Candles
guides.line: Judge acceptance by the volume in the profile, not by counting candles.
pages: VOLUME, NOT CANDLES Why the developing profile is your context for every trade THE PL AY B OOK

VOLUME, NOT CANDLES THE DE V E LOPI N G PROF ILE The Mistake Trading levels and candles, with the profile switched off in your head. One of the most common mistakes I see in the Discord: members look at candlesticks and levels only, and barely glance at the developing profile. Price comes to a level, a few candles do something, and they take the trade. That isn't how this framework works. We don't blindly trade off levels. A level only tells you where to look. The developing profile tells you what's actually happening there, and that's the context for every trade we take. W H AT THEDEVELOPINGPROFILETELLSYOUTH AT CANDLESCAN ' T 1 Where value is right now. The dVAH, dPOC and dVAL, updating with every trade. 2 Whether value is moving. Is volume building in a new area? Is the dPOC shifting? 3 Whether price is accepted or rejected. Is real business being done beyond a level, or did price just pass through? You need to keep watching how the profile develops through the session, not just check it once at the open. It's a live picture of the auction, and it changes as the auction changes. KEY TA KEAWAYA level tells you where to look. The developing profile tells you whether to trade. Never take one without the other. 2

VOLUME, NOT CANDLES THE DE V E LOPI N G PROF ILE Judging Acceptance on a Flip The mistake I see the most. For a Flip, you need acceptance beyond the level before you trade the retest. The mistake is judging that acceptance by counting candles: “there were four candles above the level, so it's accepted.” That's wrong. Acceptance means volume building beyond the level: buyers and sellers agreeing to do business at those new prices. The only place you can see that is the profile. PROFILE A ✓ PROFILE B ✗ LEVEL LEVEL Volume built above the level Accepted: this is a Flip Hardly any volume above the level Not accepted: no trade Both charts have exactly the same candles. In profile A, a real node has built above the level, so price has been accepted and the retest is a Flip. In profile B, price passed through with hardly any volume, so nothing was accepted and there's no trade. Look only at the candles and you can't tell them apart. KEY TA KEAWAY To judge acceptance, look at the volume in the profile beyond the level. The candles can't tell you. 3

VOLUME, NOT CANDLES THE DE V E LOPI N G PROF ILE It Works Both Ways Few candles can mean acceptance. Many candles can mean nothing. A few candles beyond the level doesn't mean volume hasn't been building. A lot of business can go through in a couple of bars. And the opposite is just as true: price can drift beyond a level for a long time while hardly any volume trades there. 2 CANDLES ABOVE ✓ 9 CANDLES ABOVE ✗ LEVEL LEVEL But volume built above Accepted But hardly any volume built Not accepted HOW TO CHECK FO R ACC E PTA NCE 1 Look at the profile rows beyond the level. Are they filling in, or staying thin? 2 Is a node forming there? Real acceptance builds a visible bulge of volume beyond the level. 3 Ignore the candle count. Two candles or twenty, it's the volume that decides. 4

VOLUME, NOT CANDLES THE DE V E LOPI N G PROF ILEI Don't Even Need Candles Line chart + developing profile is all the information I need. Here's how much the profile matters to me: I don't even need to look at a candlestick chart. I could trade off a line chart and the developing profile alone, and I'd still have everything I need to make the decision. CANDLES + LEVELS ONLY LINE CHART + dVP ? LEVEL LEVEL Is it accepted? You can't tell from this Volume built above the level Accepted. No candles needed On the left, it's candles and a level with no profile, and you're guessing. On the right, there are no candles at all, just a line and the developing profile, and the answer is obvious: volume has built above the level, so it's accepted. The candles were never what told you that. TRY THIS For your next session, switch one chart to a line chart and keep your developing profile and levels on. Watch how value builds and moves through the session. You'll notice how little you were really getting from the candles. KEY TA KEAWAY The candles show the path price took. The developing profile shows the auction. Trade the auction. 5

guides.title: Mind the Open
guides.line: Why I never leave limit orders sitting into a session open.
pages: MIND THE OPEN Why I never leave limit orders sitting into a session open THE PL AY B OOK

MIND THE OPEN SESSION OPENS The Open Is Different A good level can still stop you out. Most of the session, price moves through our levels in an orderly way. The auction is two-sided, volume builds, and levels get respected or accepted in a way we can read. The first minutes of a session open are different. A whole new set of traders arrives at once, and the market has to find a price that works for them. That burst of activity can slice straight through levels that would normally hold, before the auction settles down again. W H AT HAPPENS AT THEOPEN 1 Orders hit all at once. Traders who've been waiting for their market to open all act in the same few minutes. 2 Price moves fast and far. One candle can run through several levels before anyone has had time to react. 3 Stops get run. The move often goes just far enough to take out the stops sitting beyond the levels, then snaps back. So even when a level is right and price ends up reacting from it, the open can wick you out first. You were right about the level and still took the loss. KEY TA KEAWAY At the open, a level can be right and still stop you out. Don't let the open be the thing that tests it. 2

MIND THE OPEN CASE STUDY The Shanghai Open on Gold Monday 16 Nov · 09:00 Singapore time · Sunday 20:00 ET Gold reacts to the Shanghai open: China is one of the biggest gold markets in the world, and when its session opens at 09:00 Beijing time, a wave of new orders hits gold at once. GC, 1-minute chart. The circled move is the Shanghai open. Look at what happened at 20:00 ET. In one or two minutes, price dropped through the NYVAH, PWPOC, ONVAL, NYPOC and NYVAL: five levels, nearly 30 points, down below 3,865. Then it bounced straight back up through most of them. Anyone with a buy limit sitting on those levels got filled on the way down and stopped out on the wick, even though price came back above those levels minutes later. Some members learnt this the hard way today. I didn't have any limits resting into the open, so I avoided the losses completely. 3

MIND THE OPEN MY RULE Mind the Open No resting limits into a session open. This doesn't only apply to Shanghai. Every session open brings the same burst of orders: Tokyo, Shanghai, Frankfurt, London and New York. So I handle all of them the same way. HOW I HANDLE OPENS 1 Don't leave limits sitting into the open. If I have a limit order resting on a level just before an open, I cancel it. 2 Let the opening volatility settle. I wait for the spike to play out instead of being the order it runs through. 3 Re-read the developing profile. After the open, I check where volume is actually building before I trust a level again. 4 Then set the limit. Once the auction is two-sided again, the levels go back to working the way we expect. KEY TA KEAWAY Missing one trade at the open costs you nothing. Getting wicked out of five costs you the day. 4

MIND THE OPEN THEOPENS TO WAT C H Know Every Open on Your Clock Each one brings a new wave of orders into the market. These are the opens I keep an eye on. Going into each one, I don't leave limit orders resting on my levels. From my experience, gold and oil are usually the most affected during the Asian opens, so be extra careful with GC and CL around Tokyo and Shanghai. OPEN ET (WINTER / SUMMER) SINGAPORE (WINTER / SUMMER) NOTES Tokyo 19:00 / 20:00 08:00 / 08:00 Start of the Asian day. Japan doesn't change its clocks. Shanghai 20:00 / 21:00 09:00 / 09:00 Big for gold. China doesn't change its clocks. Frankfurt 02:00 / 02:00 15:00 / 14:00 The first European money, an hour before London. London 03:00 / 03:00 16:00 / 15:00 The biggest open of the European day. New York 09:30 / 09:30 22:30 / 21:30 I don't trade until 10:00 ET, so the open has passed and the developing profile has 30 minutes to build. WHY THE TIMES MOVE The US, UK and Europe change their clocks for summer, but Japan, China and Singapore don't. So the Asian opens shift by an hour in ET, and the European and New York opens shift by an hour in Singapore time. The US and Europe also change on different dates, so for a few weeks in March and October/November the gap is an hour off. Check the times in those weeks, and set alarms for the opens in your session. KEY TA KEAWAY Know when the opens are, and make sure none of them can catch a limit order you forgot about. 5

guides.title: Widen the Net
guides.line: Why you shouldn't trade one instrument forever.
pages: WIDEN THE NET Why you shouldn't trade one instrument forever THE PL AY B OOK

WIDEN THE NET CO MMONMIS TA K E Stuck on One Chart One instrument is where you start, not where you stay. A lot of members trade only one instrument every session, for months. Usually it's NQ or ES. That's exactly right when you're learning, and a mistake once you're not. As a beginner, I'd recommend focusing on just one instrument and paper trading it. Learn how it moves, how it respects levels, and how the developing profile builds. Get a feel for things before you add anything else. But once you're confident executing the setups, staying on one chart starts holding you back. That's when you move on to a few instruments. NQ, ES, GC and CL all work with this framework. 1 · Learning 2 · Executing well 3 · Confident One instrument Add a second NQ · ES · GC · CL Paper trade, get a feel Same rules, both charts More setups every session Move on when your execution is consistent, not when you get bored. KEY TA KEAWAY Learn on one. Earn on a few. 2

WIDEN THE NET WHY MORE INSTRUMENTS More Setups, More Edge Your edge needs trades to show up. Our edge only shows up over a lot of trades. On one instrument, you might only get one valid setup in a session, sometimes none. Across four instruments, you get several. More setups means the system gets more trades to realise the edge, so you get to your long-run results much faster. There's a second benefit. Some instruments are just dry on a given day. Price never comes to a level, or it's a trend day with nothing to fade. When one is dry, another one usually isn't, and it makes up for it. One session, four charts NQ Dry: nothing came to a level ES GC +1 +1 CL −1 +1 Only NQ: no trades, nothing to show for the session. All four: 4 setups, +2R KEY TA KEAWAY Same framework, same rules, more chances. One quiet chart doesn't have to mean a wasted session. 3

WIDEN THE NET THE TRADE-OFF Bigger Days Both Ways More trades means more profit potential, and more loss potential. More setups means bigger green days, but also the chance of bigger red days. That's fine, because your loss cap decides how bad a day can get, not the number of charts you watch. And over the long run, with a high win rate, more trades means you end up green more often than not. 1 : 1 AT 7 0 % · 2 - LOSSCAP 1 SETUP A SESSION 3–4 SETUPS A SESSION +0.4R +1.3R Worst possible session −1R −2R Best possible session +1R +4R Average month (20 sessions) +8R +26R Months that finish green 95% 99.9% Average result per session 40,000+ simulated sessions and months each. Trading stops for the session after 2 losses. Your worst session only goes from −1R to −2R, because the cap stops you there. But your average session more than triples, and almost every month finishes green. KEY TA KEAWAY The loss cap protects the downside. More setups grow the upside. That's the trade you want. 4

WIDEN THE NET CASE STUDY Experienced, But Stuck on One Same framework. Very different results. AMEMBERINTHEDIS CO R D This member isn't a beginner. He knows the setups, reads the developing profile well and executes cleanly. But he trades only one instrument, every session. The result: long dry spells. He's gone 3–4 days in a row without a single valid setup, just because his one chart never came to a level. Nothing wrong with his trading. There was simply nothing to trade. His upside is capped too. When the whole group was on a hot streak and setups were working session after session, he could only take the one or two his chart gave him. Everyone else was stacking wins across NQ, ES, GC and CL. He didn't get to take advantage of it. ONE INSTRUMENT HOW I TRADE (4 INSTRUMENTS) Often 0–1 3–4 on average 3–4 days Not a single session Capped by one chart Every setup, every chart Setups per session Longest run with no trades During a hot streak KEY TA KEAWAY He's already doing the hard part, reading and executing well. Widening the net is the easy part, and it's where his results are being left behind. 5

WIDEN THE NET H OW TO DOIT Adding Instruments the Right Way Grow into it. Don't jump straight to four. BEFORE YOU ADD AN INSTRUMENT 1 You're executing consistently on one. You take every valid setup at your planned size, and your journal shows you're following the rules. 2 Add one at a time. Go from one to two, get comfortable, then add the next. WHEN YOU'RE TRADING SEVERAL 1 Mark levels on every chart before the session. Same nine levels, same templates. 2 Size by risk, not by contracts. A point on GC or CL isn't worth the same as a point on NQ or ES. Keep the risk per trade the same. 3 Your loss cap covers everything. It's losses for the session, across every instrument, not per chart. 4 Respect each instrument's quirks. Gold and oil move harder, especially around the Asian opens (see Mind the Open). 5 Don't overload yourself. If two setups trigger at once and you can't manage both properly, take one and let the other go. KEY TA KEAWAY More charts, same discipline. The rules don't change. You just give them more chances to work. 6

A D VA NCEDSETUPS SETUP 04 The Anchor ⚓ The Magnet, at the old dPOC node. ADVANCED · RARE As the session builds, the dPOC can move. Volume builds at a new price, that node becomes the busiest, and the dPOC line jumps to it. But the old dPOC node doesn't disappear. If it's about as big as the current one, it's still just as much fair value. Old dPOC node Where the line was earlier About the same size dPOC moved Current dPOC Where the line is now The Anchor is a Magnet trade taken at that old dPOC node, not at the current dPOC line. O N LY TAKETHEANCHORWHENBOTHARETRUE 1 The dPOC line has only recently shifted. The move is fresh, so the old dPOC node is still live fair 2 The actual volume is similar in both nodes. Look at the bars, not the line. If the old dPOC node is clearly smaller, it isn't an Anchor. value. READ THIS LAST The Anchor builds on the Snap, the Flip and especially the Magnet. Make sure those feel obvious on your chart before you start looking for this one. 2

A D VA NCEDSETUPS SETUP 04 Why It Works We trade volume, not the line. The POC line only marks the single busiest row in the profile. When two nodes are almost the same size, a tiny difference in volume decides which one gets the line. The market doesn't care which one the line sits on. Both are prices where a huge amount of business got done. 1 Volume is what matters. An old dPOC node that's as big as the current dPOC pulls price back in exactly the same way. 2 The line can mislead you. If you only watch the dPOC line, you'll miss a Magnet that's sitting at the old dPOC node. 3 Same logic as the Magnet. Price has accepted new prices, and the retest at fair value is where you join the move. VALID ✓ NOT AN ANCHOR ✗ Old dPOC node Old dPOC node dPOC dPOC Old dPOC node about as big as the current one Old dPOC node much smaller: just an HVN KEY TA KEAWAY When the dPOC has just shifted and both nodes hold similar volume, the old dPOC node is still fair value. If it's clearly smaller, it's not an Anchor. 3

A D VA NCEDSETUPS SETUP 04 How to Trade It Same rules as the Magnet. dVAH acceptance Old dPOC node The Anchor dPOC When it's valid When it's not 1. Price builds acceptance beyond the dVAH or dVAL, exactly like the Magnet. Price snapped straight back from the dVAH or dVAL with no acceptance. No Magnet, no Anchor. 2. The dPOC line has only recently shifted, and the actual volume is similar in both nodes. The old dPOC node is clearly smaller than the current one. That's an HVN, not fair value. 3. Price comes back to the old dPOC node. Take the continuation the way price broke. EXECUTION Limit order at the old dPOC node, stop at ATR × 2 points, target 1:1, and breakeven at 75%. Same as every other setup (VP Academy #07). The Anchor is still a Magnet trade, just at the old dPOC node. Common Mistakes #06 still applies: no dPOC trades outside the Magnet. The one exception is The Guard, in the London session only (page 19). 4
